title: A contact path for a small consultancy
metaTitle: A contact path for a small consultancy
excerpt: Say what happens after they book, how soon you reply, and what to bring. The action is a working session. A ten-field form sends them back to doing it themselves.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, a long handwritten page standing in for a form that should stay short.
caption: The note they send should be shorter than a letter. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a consultancy contact page say before the form?
faqs.answer: Say what the session is, how long it is, what they leave with, and who will be in the room. Say what it is not, including a proposal tour. If the first meeting is only a fit check, call it that. Do not label a qualifying call as a working session.

faqs.question: How many fields should the form have?
faqs.answer: Stay near five: the problem, the artifact they have been rewriting, whether the decision-maker will attend, and a way to reply. Cut industry dropdowns, budget lists, and required uploads. Those ask them to do homework before they know the hour is real.

faqs.question: Should you promise a reply time?
faqs.answer: Only if you can keep it on a full week. Name the days if that is the truth. If the books are full, say the next open week before they fill the form. Do not write promptly, and do not publish an hour you will miss.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small consultancy contact page should tell a buyer who is comparing you with doing the work themselves what happens after they reach out, how soon they will hear, and what to have ready. The action is to book a working session. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them. They already have a long document. They do not need another one before they know the hour is real. Nielsen Norman Group's research is the reason to keep the page short: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds decide whether they stay. A form that looks like procurement spends that time on your process.

Write a promise you can keep. If you cannot name who replies, do not imply a principal will. If you cannot name when, do not invent a clock. A missing number is better than a number the calendar does not honor.

## What happens after they book

Say the next beats above the form or the scheduler.

They book a session of a stated length. They leave with the decision, or with a clear no from you if the problem is not one you take. The person in the room is the person who can force that decision, not a coordinator who qualifies them and disappears. A buyer who might do the work themselves is listening for a handoff. Name the role of the person they will meet.

Say what the session is not. It is not a proposal meeting. It is not a tour of your method. It is the hour in which the postponed choice gets made, or you decline. That boundary belongs above the button. If the first conversation is truly only a fit check, call it that, and do not call it a working session. The label and the hour have to match.

Put this in a few lines visible on a phone. The form comes after the promise. If you use a calendar, the event title should be the problem and the length. "Intro call" with no mention of the decision is a different product.

## How fast, only if it is true

If you reply to requests twice a week, say the days. "We confirm sessions on Tuesday and Friday" is a clock they can test. "We respond promptly" is a word they have used on themselves and not believed. Do not publish "within the hour" because it looks keen. Publish the window you can keep when you are in other sessions.

If the books are full, say the next open week before they fill a form. A hidden wait is the same delay they are hiring you to end. Honesty about capacity is part of the comparison with doing it themselves, where at least they control the calendar, badly.

If you need to see the artifact before you accept the session, say the first note only confirms receipt, and a yes or no follows after you have looked. Give the outer bound. Silence with no bound feels like the project they are already stuck in.

Read the promise in a Monday meeting until it is boring. Boring means the team can keep it. If the window slips, change the page the same day.

## What they should have ready

Ask for the minimum that lets you say yes or no, and that makes the session real.

The problem in a sentence. The artifact they have been rewriting, even if it is rough. Whether the person who can say yes will attend. A way to reply.

That is enough. You do not need company size, a budget dropdown, how they heard of you, or a briefing deck. Those belong after you have agreed the session is the right shape, and some of them belong never. Asking for a deck before the hour is how you assign them the homework they were trying to escape.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview organizes guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. This page lives on understandable. Each field needs a visible label in their words. "The decision you have postponed" is a label. "Requirements" is not. An error should say how to fix it, next to the field. Do not use placeholder text as the only label. It vanishes when they type, and it is easy to miss on a phone. Make the fields large enough to tap. A row of tiny inputs is a reason to go back to the spreadsheet.

## Why ten fields lose this buyer

Count the fields. Over five, cut. The usual excess is industry, headcount, budget, referral source, a required phone number, an upload, a privacy essay, and a newsletter box. An industry dropdown is the list you removed from the homepage, returned as a form. A free line for the problem is more honest. Budget before they have seen the fee shape turns the session into a haggle. How-they-heard-of-you is your report. Make it optional or omit it.

A required upload stops people on a phone. Let them paste the messy paragraph. You can ask for a file after you accept. A pre-checked newsletter is a dark pattern they will notice, and it confirms the suspicion that you want an audience more than a decision. Leave it off.

One short privacy sentence, with a link, is enough. Do not make consent the longest thing on the page. The longest thing should be the promise of the hour.

## The confirmation and the last ten requests

The thank-you state should repeat the promise in the same words. If you said they will meet the person who runs the session, repeat that. Do not swap in "our team." Send the same words from a named address they can reply to. A no-reply address tells them the relationship is a ticket. If you decline, decline in a sentence that restates the problem you do take. A silent archive becomes a grudge, and a grudge becomes the story they tell about consultants.

Pull the last ten inquiries, including the ones you declined. Mark every fact that changed the yes or no. If it was not on the form, add that field or admit you asked on a call. If a field never changed a decision, remove it. The form should record how you choose work. Reply to one old note using only the new fields. If you cannot, the criteria are still private. Write them down. A criterion that lives in one person's head becomes a surprise.

Do this again when the problem you take changes. An old form keeps attracting old work. The contact page is how the homepage sentence gets tested. If they disagree, fix the form the same week.

## Do not make them qualify themselves out

A buyer comparing you with their own effort is easily spooked by a form that feels like an application. "Tell us about your budget and your timeline and your stack and your team" is an application. They already suspect consultants waste time. An application confirms it before you have offered the hour. The session is the qualification. If they are the wrong problem, you say no after you have seen the sentence, not before they are allowed to speak.

Write the smallest version and use it for a month. Count how many sessions were worse because a field was missing. Add only that field. This is the opposite of copying a form from a larger firm that has a team to process leads. You do not have that team, and the buyer can tell. A short form is a claim that a principal still reads the note. If a principal does not read it, do not publish a form that pretends otherwise. Publish the email the principal actually opens, and say so.

Keep the confirmation human. "You are booked. Bring the draft you dislike. Alex will be there, and the session ends with a choice or a no." That note is worth more than a branded template full of what-to-expect paragraphs. If you cannot name Alex because you have not assigned the session, do not send the note until you can. An unassigned hour is how the page's promise dies in the inbox.

## One path

A phone number and an email can sit under the booking for people who will not use a form. They should reach the same promise. If email is the real path, do not also publish a number that goes to someone who cannot take the session. One path, with a spare door that lands in the same place.

Do not add a chat widget that opens with a greeting and no problem. It throws away the structure. Most firms cannot answer chat with the same beats as the page. Take the widget off. The page is finished when a skeptic can say what they get, by when, and what to bring, without asking you. Then remove the rest.

The next edit is usually subtraction across the whole site. Read [what to take off, starting with the industry list](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-small-consultancy) before you add a sidebar of sectors beside this form.

When you want to see a path from a first screen to a session a buyer can trust, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful pages say what happens next in the same words as the button.
